MCACN 2026 Yenko Galore: From the 1966 Corvair Stinger to the 1981 Camaro Turbo Z
12 photos
Photo: The Supercar Registry/YouTube
Opened in 1949 in Canonsburg, Pennsylvania, Yenko Chevrolet was no average dealership. In addition to selling common cars, Yenko also produced its very own vehicles. The Yenko Chevrolets are now among the most desirable performance cars from the golden era.
Yenko started out with a Durant dealership in 1929. It was opened by Frank Yenko, who in 1934 switched to selling Chevrolets. In 1957, Don Yenko, who was Frank's son, assumed ownership of the dealership. Nine years later, Yenko prepped a Corvair Corsa for SCCA racing and built 100 cars to obtain certification.
It was called the Yenko Stinger, and it was followed by many other Chevrolets through 1972. In 1981, one year before Don sold the business, Yenko produced its final batch of high-performance cars.
In all, Yenko modified five Chevrolet nameplates and rolled out vehicles for seven model years. All of them are quite rare, with production numbers ranging from a dozen to 200 units. Seeing two Yenkos at the same event is very rare, which is why the Yenko display at this year's MCACN was downright spectacular. It included one of each model built from 1966 to 1981.
Photo: The Supercar Registry/YouTube The Corvair-based Yenko Stinger is the oldest Yenko creation on display. Don completed 100 examples, which were all painted white and with blue stripes. However, the cars had different exterior mods, with some featuring fiberglass hoods and spoilers, while others came with upgraded engines. Yenko completed another 14 examples in 1967, while some sources suggest that a final car was built in 1969.
The Yenko Camaro, Don's most iconic creation, emerged in 1967. Also dubbed Yenko Super Cars, these Camaros were equipped with 427-cubic-inch (7.0-liter) V8 engines, which weren't available in the factory-built Camaro. Yenko used the L72, usually offered in the Corvette and the full-size cars.
The 1967 and 1968 Camaros were modified at Yenko's shop, but the 1969 version had its L72 installed by Chevrolet. That's because they were ordered through GM's COPO program . Yenko built 54 Camaros in 1967 and another 64 units in 1968. In 1969, Yenko ordered 198 COPO Camaros (Chevy eventually sold about 1,000 units).
The MCACN display included two 1967 Camaros, including the only known example fitted with side exhaust pipes. A 1968 Camaro and a 1969 COPO were also present, as well as a 1969 Z28 sold by the dealership (with no modifications).
Photo: The Supercar Registry/YouTube The Camaro wasn't the only Chevy that Yenko created through the COPO program. The dealership also ordered 99 Chevelles. These cars were also fitted with the 427 L72 engine. Chevrolet eventually sold a total of 323 examples. The one shown at MCACN is one of only six examples known to still exist.
1969 also saw the arrival of the Yenko Nova. Also ordered through the COPO program and fitted with the same L72 mill, the original Yenko Nova was by far the hottest compact put together in 1969. Only 38 cars were built, and one sold for a whopping $852,500 in early 2026.
Yenko rolled out a new Nova version in 1970, this time around fitted with the 350-cubic-inch (5.7-liter) LT1 V8. Unsurprisingly, Yenko used the COPO system to install the powerplant otherwise available in the Camaro Z28 and Corvette. This Nova is called the Deuce and was produced in 175 units. The MCACN display included two examples.
With muscle cars no longer popular in 1971, Yenko switched to the Chevrolet Vega subcompact. Also called the Stinger II, the Yenko Vega rolled out of the Chevrolet factory with four-cylinder engines fitted with heavy-duty forged aluminum pistons. These were designed to handle boost from the turbocharger kit offered by Yenko.
Photo: The Supercar Registry/YouTube The dealership sold 200 units per year in 1971 and 1972, with an additional unit put together as a giveaway car in 1973. That year, Yenko stopped building vehicles, opting to focus on aftermarket Stinger parts. Only 11 of the 400 Yenko Vegas are known to exist today. A 1972 example was displayed at MCACN.
In 1981, however, Yenko produced one final automobile. It was based on the 1981 Camaro Z28 and featured a body kit inspired by the IROC race cars. Power came from a 350-cubic-inch V8 engine topped by a turbocharger. The Turbo Z came with 250 horsepower on tap, which was quite impressive from the era. For reference, the factory Z28 was rated at 175 horsepower. Only 19 units were produced.
If you didn't make it to MCACN 2026, thus missing your shot at seeing every Yenko car under the same roof, the videos below include detailed walkarounds of the display. You'll also spot a 1981 Chevrolet Corvette that was sold by Yenko without aftermarket modifications. Tell me which your favorite Yenko is in the comments section below.
And in case you missed it, you should also check out the Chrysler 300 "letter series" display , which included every version of the iconic performance car built from 1955 to 1965.
